formulas.name: Present value of one cash flow
formulas.note: Mid-year convention uses the exponent n − 0.5, which always raises the value. £1.0m in 3 years at 8 % = £0.79m.

formulas.name: Annuity factor (level cash flows)
formulas.note: Multiply the annual cash flow by this instead of discounting each year. At 8 % over 5 years it is 3.99 — worth memorising.

formulas.name: Net present value
formulas.note: Positive means the project beats the discount rate. Ashdown's shop: 0.6 × 3.99 − 2.0 = +£0.40m.

formulas.name: Internal rate of return
formulas.note: No formula — find it by trial. Accept when IRR exceeds the cost of capital. The shop's IRR is 15.2 %.

formulas.name: Rule of 72
formulas.note: Doubling in 5 years implies roughly 14 %. The fastest sanity check on any IRR quoted at you.

formulas.name: Weighted average cost of capital
formulas.note: Market-value weights; (1 − t) on debt only. Ashdown: ⅔ × 14 % + ⅓ × 6 % = 11.3 %.

formulas.name: Growing perpetuity
formulas.note: C is next year's cash. £0.6m growing 2 % at 8 % = £10.0m; only valid when g < r.

formulas.name: Real vs nominal (Fisher)
formulas.note: 8 % nominal, 2.5 % inflation ≈ 5.4 % real. Match the rate to the cash flows.

formulas.name: Bond price
formulas.note: 5 % coupon, 3 years, 7 % yield = £94.75. Yield up, price down; longer bonds fall more.

canonical.a: A pound today can be invested, and a future pound might not arrive. The rate is the return available elsewhere at similar risk — it prices waiting and worry, not inflation.
Present value of the inflows minus what you spend today. Positive means the project earns more than the discount rate, so it creates value.
The discount rate at which NPV is zero — the project's own rate of return. Accept when it beats the cost of capital. It is a rate, not an amount.
The blended return every funder needs, weighted by how much each put in. It discounts unlevered free cash flow, because that cash belongs to all of them.

canonical.q: Why is equity more expensive than debt?
canonical.a: Shareholders are the residual claim — paid last, with no contract — so they demand more. Interest is also contractual and tax-deductible.

canonical.q: Why not fund everything with debt?
canonical.a: Debt lowers WACC at first, but each pound makes the equity riskier so its cost rises, lenders re-price, and distress costs appear. WACC is a shallow U.

traps: Discounting is not inflation-adjusting — it prices opportunity cost and risk. Just don't mix nominal cash flows with a real rate.
IRR is a rate, not a profit: 40 % on £10k beats nothing against 12 % on £5m.
More debt does not lower WACC forever — the cost of equity rises as leverage does.
The (1 − t) belongs on debt only; dividends are not tax-deductible.
Payback ignores the time value of money and every pound after the payback date.
Never compare cash amounts from different years without discounting them first.
Ranking projects on payback — it ignores the time value of money and every cash flow after the cut-off.
Quoting one IRR when the cash flows change sign twice — there can be two, and neither is the return.
Treating a bond's coupon as its return — the yield is set by the price.
Mixing real cash flows with a nominal rate, or vice versa.
one_liners: A pound later is a pound discounted for waiting and for worry.
NPV says how much; IRR says how fast. When they disagree, follow NPV.
WACC is what every funder together needs to be paid.
Distant cash flows don't fade — they collapse, because the discount compounds.
Payback measures speed, IRR measures rate — only NPV measures value.
The discount rate is what you could earn elsewhere at the same risk; when it rises, the most distant cash flows fall furthest.
you_may_hear: Adjusted present value (APV) — value the business unlevered, then add the tax shield separately.
Continuous compounding and the e^{-rt} form of the discount factor.
